lesson.title: The Secret History Nixon Tried to Bury
lesson.summary: In 1971, former defense analyst Daniel Ellsberg leaked a secret government study revealing that successive administrations had misled Congress and the public about the Vietnam War, setting off a landmark press freedom battle and a Nixon administration cover-up campaign that foreshadowed Watergate.
lesson.body:
In 1967, Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara, who had grown privately doubtful about the war he had helped escalate, commissioned a secret internal study of US decision making in Vietnam going back to 1945. The resulting multi-volume history, later known as the Pentagon Papers, was never meant to be seen outside a small circle of officials. Daniel Ellsberg, a former Marine and defense analyst who had worked on the study, grew increasingly disillusioned with the war as he read through the classified record of how it had been managed, and in 1971 he secretly photocopied the documents and gave them to journalists.

The New York Times began publishing excerpts on June 13, 1971. The documents showed that officials across the Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, and Johnson administrations had repeatedly given Congress and the public a rosier account of the war's prospects than internal assessments supported, even as troop levels and bombing campaigns expanded during the escalation of the mid 1960s. The revelations did not focus on the Nixon administration, which had taken office after most of the events described, but Nixon moved aggressively to stop publication anyway, arguing it threatened national security.

The Nixon administration sought a court injunction to block further publication, the first time the federal government had tried to stop a newspaper from publishing on national security grounds. The case reached the Supreme Court within weeks, and in New York Times Co. v. United States, decided in 1971, the Court ruled that the government had not met the heavy burden required to justify this kind of prior restraint on the press, allowing publication to continue and reaffirming strong First Amendment protection for the press.

Ellsberg was charged under the Espionage Act, but the case against him collapsed in 1973 after it emerged that a White House unit known as the Plumbers, formed specifically to stop leaks like this one, had illegally broken into the office of Ellsberg's psychiatrist searching for material to discredit him. That same secretive, rule breaking mindset, and some of the same operatives, would resurface the following year in a break-in at the Democratic National Committee headquarters at the Watergate complex, connecting the Pentagon Papers directly to the scandal that would eventually end Nixon's presidency.
